opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd say they've affected my thinking a great deal, probably more than I'd like to admit. For most of my career, I was someone who took AI seriously in principle. I never thought there was some magic ingredient in the human brain that a computer couldn't replicate. But in practice, I was skeptical of the hype cycles. I'd seen too many grand promises in AI that didn't pan out, so I filed it under "interesting, but probably decades away from anything that would really shake me."

Then GPT-3 came along, and I started playing with it. You could ask it to write a poem in the style of some particular poet, or explain a concept, or even attempt a proof, and it would produce something that was, okay, often wrong, sometimes ridiculous, but recognizably in the space of what a person might write. When DALL-E started producing images from text descriptions, it was the same feeling. These weren't systems built with some deep theory of language or vision. They were essentially giant neural nets trained to predict the next token, scaled up enormously. That this simple recipe went so far was, to me, one of the biggest scientific surprises of my lifetime.

So it forced me to update. If you'd asked me ten years ago whether you'd get this behavior just from scale and data, I probably would have said no. And when reality surprises you like that, the honest response isn't to find reasons why it doesn't count. It's to ask what else you might be wrong about.

That's a big part of why I became interested in AI safety, and eventually why I was willing to spend time working on it directly. Not because I'm certain about doom or anything like that. I'm still deeply uncertain about where this goes. But it became clear that this is no longer science fiction. These systems are being deployed in the world right now, and there are real questions: how do you tell whether text was produced by a model? How do you make sure these systems do what we intend? Can theoretical computer science say anything useful here? I'd like to think it can, and that's what I've been trying to figure out.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd say they've affected my thinking pretty dramatically, and I'm maybe a little embarrassed about how much. For most of my career, I was a quantum computing guy, and AI was something I'd think about occasionally, mostly from the perspective of computational complexity. And the honest truth is that if you'd asked me ten or fifteen years ago whether we'd have systems that could write a competent essay on an arbitrary topic, or produce a painting of a hedgehog in the style of Vermeer, just from a text prompt, I would have said, sure, maybe eventually, but I would not have bet on it happening in my lifetime, let alone by the early 2020s.

What's striking to me is how it happened. There was no deep conceptual breakthrough that unlocked it, nothing like what we'd want for proving P versus NP. It was basically taking an architecture, the transformer, and scaling it up by orders of magnitude on more data and more compute. And the fact that this works as well as it does, that you get these emergent abilities just from predicting the next token, is something that I think should humble everybody, including people who thought they understood intelligence.

Now, I'm also wary of overclaiming. These systems make ridiculous errors. They confabulate, they'll confidently tell you about papers that don't exist, they struggle with things a child finds trivial. So there's this weird jagged profile where they're superhuman in some directions and bizarrely incompetent in others. But I've stopped finding comfort in that, because every time I've pointed to a specific thing they can't do, a year later they can do it.

So for me the big shift is that questions I used to regard as philosophy, or as science fiction, questions about machine understanding, about alignment, about what happens when these systems get more capable, I now regard as live empirical and engineering questions. That's actually part of why I took a leave from UT Austin to spend time at OpenAI working on safety. It felt like one of those rare moments where the thing everyone's been speculating about for decades is actually arriving, and it seemed worth trying to be useful.

astra-6.text:
They’ve certainly made me update toward taking the prospect of powerful AI more seriously, and on a shorter timescale. I wouldn’t have predicted that simply scaling up these architectures would get us as far as it has. And when something surprises you, you should acknowledge that rather than immediately redefine intelligence so that whatever the computer just did no longer counts.

What’s particularly striking is the breadth. We were accustomed to computers being superhuman at a narrowly specified task, like chess. With GPT, you can ask for a poem, an explanation, or a piece of code, all through the same interface. It can fail in ways that seem ridiculous, but that doesn’t erase what’s remarkable about the things it gets right.

Now, does that mean that scaling alone will get us all the way to human-level intelligence? I don’t think we know. These systems still have problems with reliability and with maintaining a coherent chain of reasoning. But I’ve become much less comfortable making confident statements about what they won’t be able to do. The interesting question is increasingly how to understand their capabilities and limitations—and how to make sure that, as they become more capable, we can actually trust what we’re doing with them.

sol-6.1.text:
They’ve caused me to update pretty substantially. I’ve spent much of my career thinking about the limits of computation, and it’s easy, with that background, to focus on everything we don’t know how to do. Then along come these systems that do things I would have regarded as extraordinarily difficult—write coherent prose, explain a joke, generate an image from a complicated verbal description—and they do them using methods that, at a high level, are surprisingly simple.

Now, you can point out that they make mistakes, that they hallucinate, that their reasoning is unreliable. All of that is true. But I don’t think “it’s just predicting the next word” really disposes of what’s happened. Predicting the next word well enough can require learning quite a lot about the world that produced those words. The interesting question is how far that takes you, and where you need additional ideas.

So I’ve become much less confident in arguments that some particular capability is safely beyond the reach of AI. That doesn’t mean I know that scaling up these systems gets us all the way to human-level intelligence. It means that my uncertainty has increased, and I take the possibility much more seriously.
